src/data_normalization/01_carbon_emissio.module_doc_full:
CARBON INTENSITY
================
Theory
------
Carbon intensity (gCO₂/kWh) is the primary sustainability constraint for data
center siting. DC operators bound by the EU Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance,
internal Scope 2 commitments, or RE100/PPA targets must verify that the grid at
the chosen location meets their carbon budget. Grid carbon intensity is the
weighted average of emission factors across all generation technologies dispatched
in a given period, including cross-border imports:

    CI = Σ(E_i × EF_i) / Σ(E_i)

where E_i is generation from source i (MWh) and EF_i its lifecycle emission factor
(gCO₂/kWh): coal ≈ 950, gas ≈ 400, solar ≈ 30, nuclear ≈ 12, wind ≈ 15.

Why it matters for siting:
  - Hard constraint: if CI_node > operator's carbon_max, the site is ineligible
    regardless of cost or grid capacity.
  - OpEx driver: lower CI → lower Scope 2 emissions → lower EU ETS exposure and
    lower green bond financing costs (−50 to −150 bps for <100 gCO₂/kWh sites,
    EU Taxonomy aligned).

MVP Implementation
------------------
Assign the OWID/Ember national average carbon intensity to every PyPSA node in
that country. This is the direct spatial mapping approach (Approach 1 in
docs/data.md §6A):

    CI_node(n) = CI_national(country(n))

Source: OWID full energy dataset (owid-energy-data.csv), column
`carbon_intensity_elec`, last available year per ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 country code.

All nodes in the same country receive the same value. This is a valid first-order
approximation: at the national level, Ember/OWID is the most accurate and freely
available time series for EU27 + Norway.

Limitation: ignores within-country grid heterogeneity. North Germany (wind-surplus)
has substantially lower CI than south Germany (coal-dependent) — intra-national
variation of 20–30% documented in docs/data.md §6A. For national-level screening
(Filter 1 in the hierarchical approach) this is sufficient.

Future Implementation
---------------------
[Empty — to be filled in dedicated planning session]

Real implementation: PyPSA Carbon Flow Tracking (docs/data.md §3B.3). For each
bus n and simulation hour t, solve the linear system:

    CI_n(t) = [Σ G_g,n(t)·EF_g + Σ F_mn(t)·CI_m(t)] / [Σ G_g,n + Σ F_mn]

where F_mn(t) = max(0, P_mn(t)) is the import flow from neighbor m. This gives
true consumption-based Scope 2 carbon intensity at hourly nodal resolution,
accounting for cross-border electricity flows.

src/data_normalization/02_energy_price.p.module_doc_full:
ENERGY PRICE — Locational Marginal Price (LMP)
===============================================
Theory
------
Energy price is the largest single OpEx driver for a data center, accounting for
50–70 % of total operating cost over a 15-year asset life. At 50 MW load and
8,760 operating hours per year, a 10 €/MWh price difference equals ≈ €4.4 M/year
in electricity costs — the dominant variable across siting candidates.

The Locational Marginal Price (LMP) at a transmission bus is the shadow price of
the nodal power balance constraint in the Optimal Power Flow (OPF) solution. It
decomposes into three components:

    LMP_n = λ_gen + λ_loss(n) + λ_congestion(n)

  1. λ_gen:         system-wide marginal generation cost (€/MWh)
  2. λ_loss(n):     incremental I²R losses at node n (can be positive or negative)
  3. λ_congestion(n): premium/discount caused by binding transmission constraints

LMP is therefore the most precise available signal for wholesale electricity cost
at a specific grid location — it captures both fuel/carbon market conditions and
physical grid constraints (congestion rents, line losses).

MVP Implementation
------------------
Annual mean LMP from the PyPSA OPF simulation, computed as:

    energy_price_eur_mwh(n) = mean(marginal_price(n, t), t = 1 … 8760)

Source: PyPSA `n.buses_t.marginal_price` (shape: 8760 × n_buses).

Annual averaging over 8,760 hourly snapshots is a stable proxy. It smooths
short-term price spikes (e.g., gas-price events, calm-wind periods) while
preserving the structural cross-node differentials driven by persistent congestion
and regional fuel-mix differences — the signals that matter for long-horizon
siting decisions.

Diagnostic columns also exported (lmp_p05, lmp_p95, lmp_spread_p95p5) for use in
battery storage sizing and congestion analysis in downstream modules.

Limitation: The simulation year reflects a historical weather/demand year, not
current forward market prices. ETS carbon price trajectory and fuel price shocks
after the simulation cutoff are not captured. Annual-average LMP from a PyPSA
simulation year can diverge from real day-ahead market averages by 10–20 %,
mainly driven by gas price assumptions.

Future Implementation
---------------------
[Empty — to be filled in dedicated planning session]

Real implementation: pull hourly day-ahead prices from the ENTSO-E Transparency
Platform (entsoe.eu) for the last 12 calendar months per bidding zone via the
entsoe-py library, map bidding zones to PyPSA bus coordinates via spatial join,
and compute the annual average for each bus.

src/data_normalization/03_land_price.py.module_doc: LAND PRICE — Agricultural Land Transaction Prices (Eurostat apri_lprc)
src/data_normalization/03_land_price.py.module_doc_full:
LAND PRICE — Agricultural Land Transaction Prices (Eurostat apri_lprc)
=======================================================================
Theory
------
Land acquisition cost is a meaningful CapEx component for data center development,
typically 5–15 % of total project cost depending on site footprint and location.
A hyperscale DC (100+ MW) requires 20–100 ha of buildable land; site cost at
€20,000–€80,000/ha in rural EU regions adds €4 M–€8 M to project CapEx.

Agricultural land price (€/ha) is used as a DC siting proxy for three reasons:

  1. It is the only freely available EU-wide sub-national land price time series
     with consistent methodology, available at NUTS2 granularity via Eurostat
     dataset `apri_lprc` (Agricultural Land Prices and Rents).

  2. Farmland prices are driven by the same structural factors as industrial and
     commercial land prices: regional GDP per capita, infrastructure quality
     (proximity to highways, rail, fiber), development pressure, and urban
     proximity. A NUTS2 region with high farmland prices almost universally also
     has high industrial/commercial land prices.

  3. The Eurostat dataset records actual land transaction prices, not assessed or
     tax values — it reflects true market-clearing land costs in each region.

The "last 10 trades" rule applied here: average of the last 10 non-NaN annual
Eurostat observations per NUTS2 region. Each annual observation in `apri_lprc`
aggregates hundreds or thousands of individual agricultural land sales within the
NUTS2 region during that calendar year, so this equals averaging 10 annual market
clearing prices — a stable, low-volatility signal.

NUTS2 is the finest administrative level at which Eurostat consistently publishes
land transaction data. NUTS3 is available for some countries (Germany, France)
but not EU-wide. We use NUTS2 and assign the NUTS2 value to every PyPSA bus
whose centroid falls within that NUTS2 polygon (spatial join in 08_cleanup.py).

MVP Implementation
------------------
1. Fetch `apri_lprc` via the `eurostat` Python package (or REST API fallback).
2. Filter to unit=EUR_HA (price per hectare in euros) and landuse=AG (agricultural
   land, total arable + permanent grassland combined).
3. For each NUTS2 region: average of the last 10 non-NaN annual values.
4. Output NUTS2-level table. Spatial join to PyPSA nodes is in 08_cleanup.py.

Limitation: Farmland price ≠ industrial/DC land price. Urban NUTS2 regions
(Amsterdam, Frankfurt, Paris metropolitan) have scarce agricultural land and the
`apri_lprc` prices there are priced differently from commercial buildable land.
Rural regions near urban corridors may be underpriced in this proxy. This is a
first-order approximation suitable for macro-level regional screening.

Future Implementation
---------------------
[Empty — to be filled in dedicated planning session]

Real implementation: commercial real estate transaction databases (CoStar, CBRE,
JLL) or national land registry APIs (Kadaster NL, HM Land Registry UK, German
Katasteramt) for industrial/logistics land prices at municipality or cadastral
parcel level. These give true DC-site land costs but require commercial data
licenses or complex per-country API integrations.

src/data_normalization/04_infrastructure.module_doc_full:
INFRASTRUCTURE ACCESS — Grid Connection & Fiber Backhaul Proximity
===================================================================
Theory
------
Data center infrastructure access captures two distinct non-energy CapEx/OpEx
drivers that determine whether a site can be developed at all, and at what cost:

  1. HV grid connection:
     A DC drawing >10 MW must connect at ≥110 kV per EU NC DCC Regulation
     2016/1388. Connection CapEx grows linearly with distance to the nearest HV
     substation: €0.5 M–€1.2 M per km for a 110 kV aerial line, plus €1–3 M for
     the substation bay works (docs/data.md §2B). A site 5 km from the nearest
     110 kV substation adds €2.5–9 M to project CapEx before the first server
     is racked. Beyond ~10 km, grid connection cost dominates site economics.

  2. Fiber / backhaul:
     Low-latency (<10 ms RTT) fiber connectivity to an Internet Exchange Point
     (IXP) or major PoP is a hard technical requirement for DC operation. DC
     tenants pay latency-sensitive premiums; co-location clients need <4 ms to
     financial market exchanges. Fiber leasing cost (dark fiber IRU or lit service)
     grows with distance from IXP/PoP and with the number of alternative providers
     (more IXPs nearby = competitive market = lower prices).

Composite Score
---------------
Three OSM sub-signals are combined into a composite 0–1 score:

    infra_score = 0.5 × (1 − norm(dist_to_hv_substation_km))
                + 0.3 × norm(ixp_count_50km)
                + 0.2 × (1 − norm(dist_to_nearest_ixp_km))

Sub-signal 1 — dist_to_hv_substation_km (weight 0.5)
  Minimum distance (km) from the PyPSA bus centroid to any OSM
  `power=substation` node or way with parsed voltage ≥ 110,000 V (110 kV).
  Justification: direct physical CapEx driver (see above). Highest weight
  because grid connection is the single largest infrastructure variable in
  DC siting and is unambiguously measurable from OSM.

Sub-signal 2 — ixp_count_50km (weight 0.3)
  Count of OSM `telecom=exchange` nodes within 50 km radius of the bus centroid.
  Justification: OSM has no dedicated fiber backbone tag (`telecom=fiber` does not
  exist as a standard tag). `telecom=exchange` marks Internet Exchange Points and
  Points of Presence — the physical locations where fiber backbone strands converge
  (documented in docs/independent-variables.md §2, "Note on fiber proxy"). A higher
  count within 50 km means multiple fiber providers, competitive dark fiber pricing,
  and structural network redundancy. 50 km is the practical metropolitan fiber
  leasing radius in EU.

Sub-signal 3 — dist_to_nearest_ixp_km (weight 0.2)
  Distance (km) to the closest `telecom=exchange` node.
  Justification: Even if regional density is adequate, a site far from any IXP
  faces high last-mile fiber cost and latency risk. This signal is a sanity check
  complementing the count: a node could have 0 IXPs in 50 km but one at 51 km —
  the distance signal captures this.

OSM Data Coverage Note
----------------------
`telecom=exchange` tag density is positively correlated with OSM contributor
activity, not just actual fiber infrastructure. Western EU (NL, DE, FR, BE, UK)
has 5–10× higher `telecom=exchange` tagging density than Eastern EU (EE, LV, LT,
BG, RO). Nodes in the following countries receive an `infra_data_quality='sparse'`
flag: EE, LV, LT, BG, RO, HR, SI, SK, HU. These nodes should not be excluded
from candidate lists based solely on ixp_count_50km.

OSM Fetch Strategy
------------------
The script checks for an EU-wide pre-fetched cache before hitting the API:
  1. OSM_DATA_PATH env var (GeoJSON/GeoPackage with substations and exchanges)
  2. Existing data/osm_power_infrastructure.json (Luxembourg pilot — warns if used)
  3. Live fetch via osmnx per-country for all EU27 + Norway (slow, ~20–40 min)
     Results cached to data/raw/osm_eu_cache.gpkg for reuse.

MVP Implementation
------------------
Composite 0–1 score from three OSM sub-signals (see above). Normalization via
min-max across all EU nodes so the score reflects relative standing within Europe.

Limitation: OSM is a crowd-sourced dataset. Substation and IXP coverage is complete
for major transmission nodes and urban IXPs, but sparse for distribution substations
and rural telecom infrastructure. Scores in low-OSM-contributor regions (Eastern EU)
may systematically understate actual infrastructure quality.

Future Implementation
---------------------
[Empty — to be filled in dedicated planning session]

Real implementation would layer commercial data:
  - HV substation positions: TSO GIS layers (ENTSO-E, national TSOs) or the
    GridKit dataset (more complete than OSM for transmission-level substations)
  - Fiber: PeeringDB IXP database (complete, authoritative) + NLNOG Ring + Submarine
    Cable Map (TeleGeography) for long-haul routes + national dark fiber registry
    APIs where available (e.g., AMS-IX, DE-CIX, LINX public PoP lists)

src/data_normalization/05_congestion.py.module_doc_full:
CONGESTION — Grid Line Loading Fraction
========================================
Theory
------
Grid congestion measures how often a node's adjacent transmission lines are
near-saturated. It is the primary proxy for **connection queue risk** — the
probability that connecting a new large load at this node will require structural
grid reinforcement and face a multi-year queue at the TSO.

The load rate (loading fraction) of a transmission line at time t is:

    LoadRate(l, t) = |P(l, t)| / S_nom(l)

where P(l, t) is the active power flow on line l (MW) and S_nom(l) is its thermal
capacity (MVA, approximately equal to MW for EU HV lines at unity power factor).

When LoadRate > 0.80 (80 % of thermal capacity), TSOs apply operational redispatch
and typically refuse new connection applications at adjacent nodes. This 80 %
threshold is the standard N-1 operational margin: the line must retain 20 %
headroom to absorb flow rerouting following the loss of a neighboring line.

Real-world connection queue evidence (docs/independent-variables.md §3c):
  - Netherlands: zero hosting capacity at multiple substations (Mar 2026)
  - Denmark: new HV connections paused (60 GW queued vs 7.3 GW peak, Mar 2026)
  - Germany: 270 GW in connection queue, 717 applications (Q3 2025)
  - Ireland: >100 MW requires 80 % new renewable generation on-site (EirGrid 2026)

A DC connecting to a node with congestion_frac > 0.25 (lines >80 % loaded for
>25 % of the year) faces a realistic 5–10 year connection queue.

MVP Implementation
------------------
congestion_frac(n) = fraction of 8,760 annual simulation hours during which
any adjacent line of bus n exceeds 80 % of its nominal thermal capacity:

    adj(n) = {l : bus0(l) == n OR bus1(l) == n}

    congestion_frac(n) = mean_t [ max_{l ∈ adj(n)} (LoadRate(l, t) > 0.80) ]

Source: PyPSA `n.lines_t.p0` and `n.lines.s_nom`.
Formula follows docs/independent-variables.md §3b `build_grid_zone_dataset()`.

Buses with no adjacent AC lines: congestion_frac = NaN (e.g., isolated island buses,
or buses connected only via HVDC links). HVDC links are not included in this metric
because their flow is directly controlled and does not exhibit passive congestion.

Limitation: Adjacent-line proxy is a linear approximation. Real OPF redistributes
power flows network-wide via Kirchhoff's laws — actual congestion risk at a bus can
be affected by lines several nodes away. Treat congestion_frac as a first-order
screening signal; for top candidates, re-solve OPF with the new DC load added.

Future Implementation
---------------------
[Empty — to be filled in dedicated planning session]

Real implementation: N-1 security assessment. For each bus, simulate the loss of
each adjacent line one at a time and re-solve OPF, recording whether any post-
contingency line loading exceeds 100 %. Count the fraction of N-1 scenarios that
result in constraint violations. This is the standard TSO capacity assessment
methodology.

src/data_normalization/06_headroom.py.module_doc: HEADROOM — Available Grid Capacity at Node (P5 Spare MW)
src/data_normalization/06_headroom.py.module_doc_full:
HEADROOM — Available Grid Capacity at Node (P5 Spare MW)
=========================================================
Theory
------
Headroom is the spare MW capacity available at a transmission node — the maximum
load increment that can be connected without triggering structural grid
reinforcement (new lines, transformer upgrades, substation works costing
€0.5–1.2 M/km and requiring 2–7 years of permitting and construction).

For a DC developer, headroom directly answers: "Can a 50 MW DC connect here
today?" A node with insufficient headroom requires either:
  (a) A grid extension agreement with the TSO, adding years and millions to CapEx, or
  (b) A phased connection: connect at reduced power initially, then expand later
      as grid upgrades complete.

Headroom at bus n at time t is the minimum spare thermal capacity across all
adjacent AC transmission lines:

    Headroom(n, t) = min_{l ∈ adj(n)} [ S_nom(l) − |P(l, t)| ]   (MW)

where S_nom(l) is the thermal rating of line l (MVA) and P(l, t) its flow (MW).

Using the P5 (5th percentile) over 8,760 annual hours is a conservative design
choice: it means the reported headroom is available for 95 % of the year (8,322h),
while only the most extreme 438 hours (e.g., winter peak demand + calm wind events)
might exceed it. This is appropriate for a 20-year DC asset that will draw power
continuously, 24/7.

Regulatory thresholds (docs/independent-variables.md §3b scoring table):
  - headroom_mw_p05 ≥ 100 MW → GREEN  (can host a large DC without reinforcement)
  - headroom_mw_p05  20–100 MW → AMBER (possible, but reinforcement likely needed)
  - headroom_mw_p05 < 20 MW → RED    (connection requires major grid works)

MVP Implementation
------------------
headroom_mw_p05(n) = P5 of the minimum spare MW across all adjacent lines:

    spare_mw(l, t) = S_nom(l) − |P(l, t)|

    headroom_mw_p05(n) = quantile_0.05 [ min_{l ∈ adj(n)} spare_mw(l, t) ]

Source: PyPSA `n.lines_t.p0` and `n.lines.s_nom`.
Formula follows docs/independent-variables.md §3b `build_grid_zone_dataset()`.

Buses with no adjacent AC lines: headroom_mw_p05 = NaN.
Negative headroom values indicate line overloading — valid OPF results should
not produce these (OPF enforces line limits), but they can appear in unoptimized
networks; they are preserved as-is with a warning.

Limitation: Bottleneck-line proxy uses only the immediately adjacent lines.
Real OPF headroom is a function of the full network topology and can be higher
or lower than this estimate. For the top-5 candidates, re-solve OPF with the DC
load added to get a precise headroom estimate.

Future Implementation
---------------------
[Empty — to be filled in dedicated planning session]

Real implementation: DC sensitivity analysis. Inject a test load ΔP at each bus
and solve the DC power flow (linearised), recording which lines become binding.
The maximum ΔP before any line reaches its thermal limit is the true headroom.
This is computationally tractable with PyPSA's linearised DC flow model.

src/data_normalization/07_node_geometry..module_doc: NODE GEOMETRY — PyPSA Bus Voronoi Catchment Areas
src/data_normalization/07_node_geometry..module_doc_full:
NODE GEOMETRY — PyPSA Bus Voronoi Catchment Areas
===================================================
Theory
------
The atomic spatial unit for all grid scoring is the PyPSA bus catchment area —
the geographic region whose electricity grid conditions are modeled by that bus
in the PyPSA simulation. It represents a cluster of physical HV substations
whose transmission behaviour is aggregated into a single network node.

These catchment areas are defined as Voronoi tessellations of bus point
coordinates, clipped to national country borders. The Voronoi construction
ensures that any geographic location within the EU belongs to exactly one grid
node — the node of the nearest substation cluster.

Metadata columns:
  - node_id: join key to all other pipeline tables
  - x, y: centroid coordinates (REQUIRED — used by 04_infrastructure_access.py
    for spatial queries and by 08_cleanup.py for NUTS spatial join)
  - country: ISO alpha-2 — used to join carbon emissions (country-level) and
    for regulatory constraint flags
  - area_km2: Voronoi cell area in km² (EPSG:3035 equal-area projection),
    represents the geographic land mass associated with this grid node; larger
    cells correspond to sparser grid regions (Scandinavia, Eastern EU)
  - geometry: Voronoi polygon for spatial visualisation and downstream joins

Source: `resources/regions_onshore.geojson` from PyPSA-Eur Snakemake output.
Schema: name (bus id), x (longitude), y (latitude), country (ISO alpha-2),
geometry (Polygon, EPSG:4326).

Node count: ~3,000–10,000 depending on `clusters: all` network configuration.
At 256-node clustering, each zone spans ~4,000 km² (median) — too coarse for
sub-national siting. Full resolution (`clusters: all`) provides individual
substation-level nodes.

MVP Implementation
------------------
Load regions_onshore.geojson, compute area_km2 via EPSG:3035 reprojection,
rename and export. x, y centroids are explicitly preserved — they are mandatory
for all downstream spatial operations.

Limitation: Voronoi catchments are geometric approximations. Real substation
catchment areas depend on network topology and load distribution, not pure
Euclidean proximity. Voronoi cells in densely-meshed networks (Belgium, NL,
Germany Ruhr) may under- or over-represent actual grid influence zones.

Future Implementation
---------------------
[Empty — to be filled in dedicated planning session]

Real implementation: compute influence zones via power transfer distribution
factors (PTDF) or sensitivity analysis — each bus's catchment is the set of
grid points where injection from that bus most strongly determines the LMP.
This is mathematically correct but computationally intensive.

CLEANUP — Validation, Spatial Join, and Processed Dataset Export
=================================================================
This script:
  1. Loads all raw parquet files from data/raw/
  2. Performs the NUTS2 spatial join to assign land_price_eur_ha to each node
  3. Validates all scoring columns for schema correctness and value ranges
  4. Saves cleaned tables to data/processed/

No normalization happens here — raw values are preserved.
The final assembly into grid_nodes.parquet is performed by 09_build_table.py.

src/data_normalization/09_build_table.py.module_doc_full:
BUILD TABLE — Final Dataset Assembly
======================================
Imports all processed parquet files from data/processed/, merges them on node_id,
and writes the final analysis-ready dataset to data/grid_nodes.parquet.

Output schema:

  Metadata columns (not scored):
    node_id             str       PyPSA bus index
    x                   float     Centroid longitude (EPSG:4326)
    y                   float     Centroid latitude  (EPSG:4326)
    country             str       ISO alpha-2
    area_km2            float     Voronoi cell area  (EPSG:3035, km²)
    geometry            Polygon   Voronoi cell polygon (EPSG:4326)

  Scoring columns (raw values):
    energy_price_eur_mwh    float   Annual mean LMP (€/MWh) — PyPSA
    land_price_eur_ha       float   Avg of last 10 annual values (€/ha) — Eurostat
    carbon_intensity_elec   float   National carbon intensity (gCO₂/kWh) — OWID
    infrastructure_access   float   Composite OSM score 0–1
    congestion_frac         float   Fraction of hours >80% loading (0–1) — PyPSA
    headroom_mw_p05         float   P5 spare capacity on adj lines (MW) — PyPSA

All scoring columns may be NaN where the upstream source is unavailable
(PyPSA-dependent columns are NaN if no network file was provided).
